analysis.one_liner: Reserves Pacific Northwest old-growth forests from logging while guaranteeing timber sales and retraining aid for displaced timber workers.
analysis.headline: The Ancient Forest Act of 1991 was heard in House subcommittees but never reported out of committee and never got a floor vote, dying when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set aside roughly 6.3 million acres of federal old-growth forest in Oregon, Washington, and Northern California as a reserve system where logging and most vegetation removal would be banned, to protect the northern spotted owl and old-growth ecosystems. At the same time, it guaranteed minimum federal timber sales of at least 2.2 billion board feet a year from national forests and 450 million board feet from Bureau of Land Management lands during a three-year transition, and doubled the share of timber receipts paid to affected counties from 25% to 50%. It also created a timber worker retraining program funded by 5% of federal timber receipts, community assistance task forces, and hiring preferences for local workers on federal forest restoration projects.
analysis.who_benefits: The American public gains permanent protection of old-growth forests for recreation, biodiversity, and water quality, plus endangered-species protection for the northern spotted owl. Timber workers displaced by reduced harvests gain a federally funded retraining program with job search and relocation allowances. Counties containing the affected forests gain doubled payments, 50% instead of 25% of timber receipts, for five years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, timber workers, and rural counties

how_it_helps.text: Would designate a Pacific Northwest Ancient Forest Reserve System of roughly 5.66 million acres of national forest and 660,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management lands, where vegetation removal is prohibited except for public safety, recreation, and administration.

Would require reserves to include at least half of the remaining old-growth ecosystems in the Douglas-fir region and lands needed for the recovery of the northern spotted owl, based on the 1990 Interagency Scientific Committee report.

Would create a Timber Worker Adjustment Program under the Job Training Partnership Act, funded by 5% of federal timber receipts, providing training, job search allowances up to $800, and relocation allowances to workers laid off because of federal timber decisions.

Would raise county payments from national forests in the region from 25% to 50% of receipts for five years and establish local task forces, grants, and a presidential coordinator to help timber-dependent communities diversify.
Would require timber sales to be offered from lands with the least ecological impact first, and ban sales in specified habitat and old-growth areas during the transition.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry would lose access to roughly 6.3 million acres of federal old-growth forest where logging would be banned, reducing the federal timber supply that mills in the region depend on. Federal agencies would bear the cost of administering the reserves, the research program, and community assistance, partly through a 5% diversion of timber receipts and new appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Northwest timber mills and logging operations

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates minimum timber sale volumes of at least 2.2 billion board feet per year from national forests and 450 million board feet from BLM lands for fiscal 1992-1994, locking in continued logging of old-growth lands outside the reserves regardless of later scientific findings.
Reserve boundaries could only be changed by an Act of Congress, making the protection rigid even if science or conditions changed.

The retraining and county-payment programs are funded from timber receipts and new appropriations, meaning the transition aid depends partly on continued logging, and the economic diversification effort might not replace lost timber jobs in isolated communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine compromise bill: it traded permanent protection of the largest remaining old-growth stands for guaranteed timber volumes, doubled county payments, and a worker retraining fund, trying to soften the blow to timber towns and mills. The mandated timber floors and the dependence of worker aid on logging receipts weaken the environmental side of the bargain, but the reserve system would still have been one of the largest old-growth protections ever enacted. The main honest objection from supporters of full protection is the guaranteed sales; the main objection from the industry is the scale of the reserves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and its subcommittees held hearings, but no committee ever reported it to the floor; in May 1992 the record pointed readers to a different bill, and the Congress ended in January 1993 without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the bill on March 21, 1991 with 20 original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Education and Labor Committees.
It gathered 24 cosponsors, 22 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and was referred to subcommittees on Forests, Department Operations, and National Parks and Public Lands.
Subcommittees held hearings in April and May 1991, and in July 1991 the committees requested executive comment from the Interior Department and USDA, but the bill was never marked up or reported.
On May 7, 1992 the action record added a notation 'See H.R.4899', pointing to separate legislation, and the bill died without a floor vote when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Pacific Northwest timber industry, which kept unrestricted access to old-growth federal lands for the rest of the Congress rather than facing a reserve system with guaranteed but reduced timber sales; no permanent old-growth reserve system was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Northwest timber industry kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ancient Forest Act of 1991 and led it through referral to three committees.

for.name: 24 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 22 Democrats and 2 Republicans, giving the bill bipartisan support.

for.name: National conservation organizations
for.role: Environmental groups supporting spotted owl and old-growth protection
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed Congress throughout this period to protect the northern spotted owl and remaining ancient forests, the issue this bill addressed.

against.name: House Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Education and Labor Committees
against.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings but never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for floor action.

against.name: Pacific Northwest timber industry
against.role: Mills, logging contractors, and timber-dependent businesses
against.what_they_did: Opposed major reductions in old-growth timber harvest from federal lands in the region during this fight.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Preferred its own administrative spotted owl planning over legislatively mandated reserve systems, and the agencies' comments were still pending when the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily Democratic, 22 of 24 cosponsors, though two Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committee rather than failing on a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would have banned logging on roughly 6.3 million acres of reserve land but simultaneously guaranteed minimum federal timber sales of over 2.65 billion board feet a year through 1994 and required continued 'New Forestry' harvest outside reserves, keeping mills supplied at a reduced level. The industry's interest in maximizing old-growth harvest ran against the public's interest in protecting the last uncut forests, and with the bill's death the industry kept the unrestricted status quo.

The bill would have doubled county payments from 25% to 50% of federal timber receipts for five years and channeled grants, loans, and a 5% timber-receipt set-aside into worker retraining and economic diversification. County residents are the same ordinary people the bill's worker programs aimed to help.
